nexusClaim.associationBasis: Authoring registers this relationship only as the bounded association the located bidirectional literature supports, with the direction limits stated first: a 2008 systematic review of prospective studies that excluded prevalent cases in each direction reports the pooled relative risk for INCIDENT DEPRESSION in baseline type 2 diabetes as 1.15 (95 percent CI 1.02-1.30, seven studies, 6,414 incident cases), while the REVERSE direction is stronger (incident diabetes in baseline depression RR 1.60, 95 percent CI 1.37-1.88, thirteen studies, 6,916 incident cases), so the relationship is explicitly bi-directional with the claimed direction the weaker of the two (PMID 19033418); and a 2001 meta-analysis of 42 studies reports the odds of comorbid depression twice that of nondiabetic comparison groups (OR 2.0, 95 percent CI 1.8-2.2, twenty controlled studies), with prevalence higher in diabetic women (28 percent) than men (18 percent) and strongly assessment-method dependent (31 percent by self-report versus 11 percent by standardized diagnostic interview) (PMID 11375373). The registered claim is the narrowest these anchors jointly permit: that type 2 diabetes is associated with a MODEST elevated risk of incident depression and with doubled comorbid-depression odds, with the reverse direction carrying the larger effect and no anchor establishing that the diabetes caused any individual's depression.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation of depression is established for any individual: the prospective meta-analysis reports only a MODEST relative risk of 1.15 in the claimed direction while the reverse direction is 1.60, and its own authors call for research into mechanisms, so the located evidence supports a bidirectional association rather than a one-way diabetes-to-depression pathway; the comorbidity anchor is a prevalence meta-analysis whose odds ratio cannot set direction at all and whose prevalence estimates swing from 11 to 31 percent purely on assessment method, so instrument choice explains much of the measured burden; depression in diabetes is plausibly mediated by complication burden, diabetes distress, lifestyle constraint and vascular disease, none of which the anchors separate from a direct effect of the diabetes itself. Individual claims require independently established type 2 diabetes and separately diagnosed depressive disorder with dated onset records, exclusion of diabetic complication burden and vascular depression, of diabetes distress and adjustment disorder, of medication effects (corticosteroids, statins, interferons) and of pre-existing psychiatric history before any attribution.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized multifactorial pathway: chronic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance are held to affect central monoaminergic function and neurotrophic signaling while the lifestyle and complication burden of diabetes sustains depressive arousal, a composite route consistent with the modest prospective RR of 1.15 and with the doubled comorbid odds but NOT separable within the located designs; whether diabetes produced any individual's depression rather than the reverse (the stronger direction) or a shared metabolic-vascular-psychosocial substrate remains hypothesized until the two diagnoses' chronology is read together.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Held at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at prospective-meta-analysis and comorbidity-meta-analysis class with the bidirectional asymmetry carried as the controlling limitation: the claimed direction (RR 1.15) is the WEAKER half of an explicitly bidirectional relationship whose other half (depression to diabetes, RR 1.60) is stronger, so this edge is registered narrow and the reverse route is NOT claimed; the comorbidity anchor is direction-blind and assessment-method sensitive (31 percent self-report versus 11 percent diagnostic interview); a published critique of the prospective anchor exists (comment in Diabetes Care 2009;32(5):e56, with author reply e57) whose content was NOT reviewed here and which a qualified human must read before the edge lands. Target note: the catalog carries diabetes-mellitus-type-2 with three registered suggestions and depressive-disorder with very many registered incoming windows, so this edge adds one more mood window rather than a new mechanism class and no parallel-targeting pair is created.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The claimed direction is the weaker half of a bidirectional association (RR 1.15 versus 1.60) and no anchor isolates a diabetes-specific causal effect from complication burden, diabetes distress and shared vascular-psychosocial risk; the prospective anchor covers only seven studies and 6,414 incident cases in this direction and is subject to a published critique whose content is unreviewed here; the comorbidity anchor cannot set direction and its prevalence varies threefold by assessment method; and no anchor reports depression incidence stratified by glycemic control or complication status.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Depression predating the diabetes diagnosis (the stronger reverse direction, RR 1.60)
Diabetic complication burden, neuropathic pain and vascular disease as mediators rather than the diabetes itself
Diabetes distress and adjustment disorder rather than major depressive disorder
Medication effects including corticosteroids, and chronic medical illness burden
Shared metabolic-vascular-psychosocial risk substrate producing both conditions without a direct link

sourceReferences.citation: Mezuk B, Eaton WW, Albrecht S, Golden SH. Depression and type 2 diabetes over the lifespan: a meta-analysis. Diabetes Care. 2008 Dec;31(12):2383-2390. doi:10.2337/dc08-0985. PMID 19033418.
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of prospective comparative studies excluding prevalent cases in each direction, registered as the PRIMARY anchor and the only direction-capable anchor: diabetes predicting incident depression RR 1.15 (95 percent CI 1.02-1.30, seven studies, 6,414 incident cases); depression predicting incident diabetes RR 1.60 (95 percent CI 1.37-1.88, thirteen studies, 6,916 incident cases). The claimed direction is the weaker half of an explicitly bidirectional relationship and that asymmetry is carried on every face of the held edge. DISCLOSURE CARRIED: a published critique exists (comment in Diabetes Care 2009;32(5):e56, author reply e57) whose content was NOT reviewed here and must be read before landing. Mapping approval is not citation verification; this source enters verified:false pending qualified-human citation review.

sourceReferences.citation: Anderson RJ, Freedland KE, Clouse RE, Lustman PJ. The prevalence of comorbid depression in adults with diabetes: a meta-analysis. Diabetes Care. 2001 Jun;24(6):1069-1078. doi:10.2337/diacare.24.6.1069. PMID 11375373.
sourceReferences.note: Meta-analysis of 42 studies (20 with nondiabetic comparison groups), registered as the MAGNITUDE-CONTEXT anchor: odds of depression twice the nondiabetic comparison group (OR 2.0, 95 percent CI 1.8-2.2), stable across sex, diabetes type, subject source and assessment method in the controlled studies; prevalence 28 percent in diabetic women and 18 percent in men, and highly assessment-method dependent (31 percent self-report versus 11 percent standardized diagnostic interview). LIMITATIONS CARRIED: a prevalence meta-analysis cannot set direction, and its prevalence swings threefold on instrument choice.
